html:
"Eastern Masurian culture" is the map's label, from 500 BCE to 100 CE, for the Iron Age people of eastern Masuria and the lands toward the Neman River, in today's northeastern Poland, southern Lithuania and western Belarus.

What is known comes from archaeology, and the map's split into a western and an eastern culture is a simplification. Western Masuria belonged to the West Baltic Kurgans culture; to the east and northeast lay the hillforts and villages of the Brushed Pottery culture. People in this belt farmed small fields, kept cattle and pigs, fished in the many lakes and hunted in the forests. They cremated their dead.

They spoke early Baltic languages. In later centuries this land was home to the Sudovians, also called the Yotvingians, a warlike Baltic people whose name may appear in Ptolemy as the Soudinoi in the 100s CE. They held out against Poles, Rus' and crusaders until the Teutonic Knights conquered them in the 1280s, and their language later died out. Their western neighbours on the map were the Western Masurian culture.
